title: Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
content: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin. The 71-year-old underwent a 90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. "The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it added. The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks". The Pope is expected to remain in hospital for about a week. Earlier, large crowds waited for hours outside the hospital for the Pope. They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car. He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured. In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical". A Vatican source told Agence France-Presse news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread. It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing. He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed. Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness. Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically. He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan. The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years. Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world. "Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday. He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery. Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted. Carla had come specially, wanting to be close. "He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray." "I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff. "It turns out he's vulnerable too," she added. The 31-year-old cave expert was found alive, 32ft underground, after more than 100 emergency personnel worked to free him. The 71-year-old pontiff said the nodule was identified "at a very early stage". Dramatic footage shows huge tornado moving through Marsala and Petrosino, causing damage to buildings and cars. The heist at the Florence-based winery is believed to be one of the largest thefts of its kind in Italy. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the move will deliver more stable government, but opposition parties say her aim is to stay in power. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on alleged espionage
content: Russian authorities have charged a Japanese journalist for espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo. The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun, was detained in Russia's far eastern region of Sakhalin, a day before he was due to leave the country. The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands , claimed by both countries, in August. Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities are "verifying the facts" and will "respond appropriately" thereafter. Russian authorities allege that Imai had "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported. The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. Imai has been taken to Moscow and will be remanded until 12 December, before the trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency. Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be jailed up to 20 years in prison. "Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday. "We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity. Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin. Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter, but did not comment further on the incident. Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. Takaichi slammed Putin's visit in August – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories". Moscow dismissed her criticism as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded". Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo for requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese. The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine. In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison. Gershkovich, a US citizen, was in 2024 released in a prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War took place. In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours. Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. It comes after Andy Burnham said Moscow had tried to interfere in the 2016 referendum. Sir Ken McCallum says operations to tackle terrorism and state threats are now roughly of an "equal scale". Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says. As election day looms, the president turns his eyes overseas for help with a pressing domestic problem. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
content: Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites. The activists climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday. The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies. Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny. Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody to help the police further investigate the charges, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. Das and Ranka have the option of seeking bail from a higher court. The arrests follow an earlier round of detentions over the weekend, when CJP leaders were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations in the capital before being released by a magistrate. The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission has denied wrongdoing. Delhi police have name three other sites in the city - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground - as protest venues. The CJP says the move will make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard. On Tuesday, CJP founder Abjijeet Dipke and other leaders shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar. Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades while chanting slogans and holding the Indian flag. "You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X. Following their detention, Ratna Singh, the head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours and were taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time [21:30 GMT on Tuesday]. The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms. The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change. After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability. The Hokkaido Shimbun journalist is accused of collecting information on Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo. Anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning land in Indonesia and the authorities who have failed to stop them. A new industry being dubbed the “loneliness economy” has emerged in China, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly. "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC. A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and civilian resistance. title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
content: "The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV." Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia. "I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer." Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner. Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact". There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country. But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives. Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that. "We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs. "For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine." "The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added. Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver. The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible. His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows. There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles. Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile. "After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC. She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult. But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood. "I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him. Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits. Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic. "Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards." She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves. "So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious." At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection. Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee. "If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect." Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province. "We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said. The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month. He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said. "We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her." After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude. "The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback." Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity. Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly. "It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said. "I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy. "I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart." Stephen Gilbert, 74, was born with unilateral microtia, a rare condition in which the external ear is underdeveloped or missing on one side. Jo Goldsmith said the RSV vaccine was not available when she was pregnant, but that she would have had it. title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
content: Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town. Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less. According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror. "The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon. Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored. While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding. On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area. To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental. For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa , where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release. "The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House. "I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party." The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody. Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September , accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since. Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years. The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated. With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities? "The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council. "There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government." The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics. Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion. But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party. "The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says. Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision. "The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says. Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks. "The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally." But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most. The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India. Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous. Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame. "I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands." "It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan. Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues. "If they're going to launch these operations, they're going to have to be prepared to accept casualties of members of the armed forces," she says. If those are significant, it could lead to questions inside the military institution, she adds. Pakistan, with its history of military coups, has examples in its past where removing elected governments, whether provincial or national, can turn sour. "It's not that senior people in the PML-N [the party in federal government] don't realise that some of these things can come back and haunt them in the future," Noor says. "Similarly I think to some extent the PTI realises that they will not be able to hold a protest and get Imran Khan out. I think that's the most unfortunate part of this mess that we're in, that we are going into it with our eyes wide open. "Everybody realises that this is a train crash but somehow you can't stop it." Thousands have taken to the streets after talks between authorities and Khan's party ended in deadlock. Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests. The former skippers say it is "basic decency" for Pakistan to comply with a court-ordered medical assessment. It comes as the court had earlier this week ordered that he had to be taken for a hospital examination. Imran Khan has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption charges which he says were politically motivated. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Sydney teen charged with murder of boy who was shot in face
content: Australian police have charged a 19-year-old man with murder after a boy, aged 12, was fatally shot in the face and neck at a Sydney home last month. Police were called to a unit in Sydney's northwest on 21 September after reports of a shooting. The boy was rushed to hospital in a critical condition and died three days later. Nine people at the home when the shooting happened were uninjured. Three men - all aged 18 - were arrested and two later released without charge. The third man, Isaac Bechara, who has since turned 19, was initially charged with concealing a serious indictable offence and remanded in custody. On Tuesday, police charged him with murder. Bechara did not apply for bail when he appeared in court on Wednesday. In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, New South Wales (NSW) police ruled out links to organised crime but days later, investigators said they were looking at possible gangland connections. "A number of individuals that were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW Police and their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators," said Supt Naomi Moore last month. Moore added that some of the people who were present at the time of the shooting were "not currently co-operating with investigators" and that police were yet to recover the firearm. Local media reported that the incident was a suspected accident, citing police sources, and that the boy's father had paid tribute to his son on social media, posting a photo of the pair with the caption, "RIP my baby". When the boy's death was announced, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said any incident "where we lose a young life in those circumstances is tragic". Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment". A man's confession to abducting UK toddler Cheryl Grimmer in Australia was previously thrown out. Wednesday's fatal shooting of a man in his 40s comes after a university student was gunned down on Tuesday. Cheryl Grimmer's family have been petitioning police to consider the new evidence they say they've found. Julian Ingram is wanted over the shooting deaths of three people, including his pregnant former partner. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
content: A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners". Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people had been killed and 21 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. He said "several energy facilities" in Kyiv had been hit in what he, without giving more detail. Kyiv has reported multiple Russian strikes since US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine two days ago. In the early hours of Wednesday, Klitschko said the "massive missile attacks" had knocked out power to parts of Kyiv. Kyiv officials have urged residents to stay in shelters after declaring a red alert due to a "missile threat". Following the strikes on Tuesday, Zelensky said: "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people. "This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added. "It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing." It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv. Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case. "We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said. "We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end." Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before." But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there". It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow ⁠his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president". Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war. CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war. It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down. That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters. Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. Six crew members are rescued but 10 are missing after a merchant ship was sunk overnight, Bulgaria says. Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says. As election day looms, the president turns his eyes overseas for help with a pressing domestic problem. While Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggests he would sign up to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, Russia has said little. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
content: The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say. They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built. The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside. The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. "The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition. The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves. Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae. The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age. Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, differerent styles are linked to particular periods. The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base. Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old. "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%." Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater. Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue. "I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said. The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae. "It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said. "It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years." The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world. The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. They believe is it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete. Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships. There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaelogy Association specialises in finding and studying them. Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel. "We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years. "We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back." The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks. Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago. The oldest known shipwreck where some of the wood is still preserved was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago. The tettine was found in an archaeological dig about 15 years ago but has only just been restored. The "rare" and "very unusual" skull was discovered in a cave on the Mendip Hills. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Archaeologists hope to uncover more fragments of the medieval site in Perth. The Belgian ship Z.592 Hosanna disappeared in February 1980 while on a European voyage from Devon. Copyright 2026 BBC. title: One stolen every four minutes - inside the police battle against vehicle thieves
content: It is 01:00 on a Thursday and we are in the back of an unmarked police car on the hunt for vehicle thieves in east London. A call comes in over the radio about a stolen Ford Transit van. Within 25 minutes officers have found it, chased it down and arrested a suspect. Officers tell us the night has been successful, with further arrests made, yet across the UK a car is stolen every four minutes. Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to Home Office data. Last year, just 3% of vehicle theft offences resulted in a charge or summons. As well as spending time on the front line in London and Sussex, we have privately spoken to 20 police officers from six forces. They told us while they have the skills and experience to tackle vehicle crime, they are overstretched, under-resourced and struggling to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminal networks. Thieves are becoming more confident. A man who claims he receives stolen vehicles and breaks them into parts at a so-called "chop shop" told the BBC he does not fear the authorities, because they "couldn't catch a cold". Once the preserve of joyriders and opportunists, vehicle theft is now a lucrative global criminal business. Cars are stolen to order, and moved across the country or dismantled within hours, say police, making them difficult to recover and suspects hard to track. Many vehicles are sent overseas to places like the United Arab Emirates, The Democratic Republic of Congo and Jamaica. Victims of car theft have told us they feel frustrated and helpless. One woman said it took car thieves just 35 seconds to steal her BMW, yet police only began investigating a day later. Another man said he feared for his life when masked thieves broke into his home demanding his car keys. The success criminals are having is also hitting motorists more widely, with insurance quotes having risen by 82% since 2021, according to security think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi). Our night-time ride in the unmarked police car takes place during an eight-hour Metropolitan Police operation targeting vehicle crime. "Havering has been affected quite badly," PC Yoosef Outaleb tells us - partly because thieves use the back roads as a cut-through to neighbouring Essex. Police say the county has particularly high numbers of illegal "chop shops", which dismantle vehicles for parts so they can be sold and exported. "They [the criminals] don't have borders, whereas we do," he says. When criminal activity straddles police force boundaries, investigations can often slow down - which gangs look to exploit. Two stolen vehicles are recovered, yet Met officers also uncover other crimes. They pursue armed robbers on e-bikes, apprehend a drunk driver and arrest three men in a car full of Class A drugs, cash and phones. It is all important work, but police admit that responding to these crimes diverts them away from targeting known vehicle thieves. The thieves, known as "grafters" within criminal networks, are out every night stealing cars, the man claiming to work at a chop shop told us. Many vehicles are then broken into parts. Such is the demand, he says, that deals to re-sell the parts are often done before he has even finished dismantling a vehicle. Some stolen vehicles are left intact, given new number plates and sold in the UK or abroad, while others are used to facilitate drug dealing and human trafficking, or as getaway vehicles for robberies and break-ins. While the long-term trend presents difficult reading for police, reported vehicle thefts fell 5% in England and Wales last year, to 119,000. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, vehicle thefts remained largely flat, at about 5,000 and 1,200 a year respectively. Fifteen of the 32 police forces in England and Wales that responded to a BBC Freedom of Information request said they do not employ any full-time, specially-trained stolen vehicle examiners, who can carry out detailed examinations of cars and bolster investigations. But Assistant Chief Constable Sarah Grahame, the national police lead on tackling vehicle crime, tells us officers' efforts - like the night-time operation in east London - are having an impact. UK forces are also collaborating with Interpol, shipping companies and vehicle manufacturers to address an issue "that spans globally", she says. She admits current theft levels are unacceptable, but says there is no funding to routinely carry out large-scale operations within current police budgets, set by the Home Office. Instead, forces organise "intensification weeks" aimed at disrupting criminal networks. One involving 32 forces last month, called Operation Alliances, led to at least 286 arrests and 319 vehicles seized. In East Sussex in September, where we witnessed a smaller, targeted operation, we were told that 17 cars had been stolen in the Hastings and Rother areas in the previous two months. Many of the vehicles were keyless Toyota RAV4s - taken by thieves using technology that bypasses vehicle security systems. Three of the vehicles had been taken the previous night. Within hours, officers recovered all three vehicles and arrested three suspects, including one they believe had been in charge of the other two. Two suspects have now been charged, including one arrested after a stolen Toyota was found near his home. Sussex vehicle crime lead Ch Insp Oliver Fisher, says police resources are now being focused on "the top of that criminal network... that's where you'll seize the most assets and cause the most disruption". Without catching criminal bosses, experts agree, others lower down will continue carrying out thefts to order - often using tech such as cloned keys to access vehicles. Manufacturers need "a constant focus on security", says Thatcham Research - a body that works with carmakers, police and government to improve vehicle security. "Within months" of a car being launched, thieves can develop targeted tools to steal it, it says. At Thatcham Research's headquarters, we are shown a device hidden within a wireless speaker that can start a car by tapping into its internal communication system. We also see a military-grade signal jammer, left behind by criminals after a theft, that can block out all electronic signals for miles around. While manufacturers are meeting security guidelines, the government should update regulations to ensure "sophisticated [theft] countermeasures are on a vehicle as standard", says Thatcham Research's principal engineer for automotive security, Steve Launchbury. Tech that puts a key to sleep while motionless is one option, he says, so thieves cannot hack into it. In future, it may be possible for manufacturers to remotely lock down a car reported by the owner as stolen, he adds. The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders told us car makers go "above and beyond regulatory requirements", while Toyota said it "continuously enhances vehicle security". Mike Bull, 33, believed he had done everything he could to prevent his BMW M3 from being taken. He had CCTV, a house alarm and a protective container for his keys. But just two months after he bought the car, two masked men broke into his home in the middle of the night and demanded the keys. "I was kind of scared for my life," he says. Avon and Somerset Police says it is "following up all lines of enquiry", but his car has not been recovered. Rose-Marie Clarke has been a victim of car theft twice in three years. Most recently, in March, her BMW was stolen from outside her home using an antenna to amplify the signal from the key fob inside her house. It took thieves just 35 seconds. Clarke, like many victims we have spoken to, is critical of the police. She says officers told her they knew the likely suspect, who had recently been released from prison, but they had been unable to prove it was him. "It's disheartening… you feel powerless because the police are powerless," she says. Warwickshire Police said despite "extensive enquiries… an offender could not be identified". BMW UK said it worked "continuously" to improve security. Many victims we spoke to told us they had also been hit hard by a rise in their car insurance premiums. Across the UK, car insurance quotes have risen by 82% since 2021 and Eli Glantz, an expert in organised crime and policing at security think tank Rusi, says vehicle crime "is certainly a factor". "As more vehicles are stolen, insurers are forced to pay out more often. Premiums are going to rise," he adds. Vehicle crime costs the UK economy £1.7bn a year, Rusi estimates. Since April, it has been an offence to possess electronic devices used in vehicle thefts, but Glantz believes legislation is still failing to keep pace with the criminals. It is welcome, he says, that the government is now giving vehicle thefts more attention, but he stresses that current police resources will not meaningfully reduce the number of crimes. Several of the police officers we spoke to privately felt similarly. They said they had confidence in their ability to take down serious, organised vehicle crime networks, provided they had the necessary level of funding and support from decision-makers. The Home Office says it "will continue to support police" in tackling organised vehicle theft and provides £300,000 a year to help strengthen its response, mainly to the National Vehicle Crime Reduction Partnership. Investigations reporter NJ Convery has been out on a nighttime hunt for vehicle thieves. The vehicle overturned near Angmering in the early hours, causing delays. title: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
content: In China's cities, despite the huge crowds, or maybe because of them, residents can feel very isolated. Now, a new industry being dubbed the "loneliness economy" has emerged, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly. The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell visits a company that does just that, to see how their business works. Read more about the paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely. Reports say a gas leak at a fried chicken shop may be behind the blast, which killed two and injured 26. With Super Tuesday underway in the US, the BBC asks China's elite who they want to win this year's election. At least nine people were injured in the incident, which Chinese state media said involved over 100 cars. A trained economist, Li was once tipped to be the country's future leader. The highest level of storm alert is in effect in Hong Kong, with people being warned to stay indoors. China police issue warnings after a child is seen playing hide and seek on the side of a apartment building. Giant panda at Wolong Shenshuping, China, looks very relaxed whilst they have the hiccups Video from China’s Sichuan province shows the animal looking relaxed, but unimpressed. The rescue was shown on Chinese state TV as devastating floods hit Hebei province. Parts of China have been hit by an onslaught of extreme weather, causing widespread flooding. This video has been removed for rights reasons. The blast was caused by a leaking liquefied petroleum gas tank, state media reports. Harrowing video shows people trying to escape a fire in Beijing that killed 29 people. On land, by sea and in the air - pictures released by China's state broadcaster show military drills around Taiwan. The BBC's Celia Hatton breaks down Xi Jinping's caffeine habits, and why they might be a subtle power play. As China deals with a new Covid wave, Ros Atkins looks at why it’s hard to assess its scale. Jimmy and Tommy Lindesay are covering the equivalent of a marathon every day for six months. People in Beijing see a cautious return to life after China lifts its most severe Covid restrictions. There were widespread protests after 10 people died in a tower block fire in the city of Urumqi. title: Pictured: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
content: An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain. Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females. For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals." He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said. The competition's annual exhibition opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images. Category : Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years Photographer : Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK Location : Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required. While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task. "I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield. Category : 10 Years and Under Photographer : Amelie Davis, UK Location : Surrey, England You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone. The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower. Category : Animals in their Environment Photographer : James Lewin, UK Location : Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared. Category : Animal Portraits Photographer : Aaron Sanders, UK Location : Porthkerris Beach, Cornwall Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased. Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity." Category : Birds Photographer : Isak Pretorius, South Africa Location : Mabamba Swamp, Uganda Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two – likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest. Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Category : 15-17 Years Photographer : Konrad Gräeter, Germany Location : Baden-Württemberg, Germany Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate. This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions. Category: Urban Wildlife Photographer: Seth Forestson, UK Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline. These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi. Category: Under Water Photographer: Tony Wu, USA/Japan Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, Kyūshū, Japan This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said. Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance. Category: Photojournalist Story Award Photographer: Loren Elliott, USA Location: USA San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed. Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles Photographer: Anton Sorokin, US Location: Contra Costa County, California, USA Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs. Category : Behaviour: Invertebrates Photographer: Sitaram Raul, India Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert. Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat. Category: Oceans: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Lindbloom, USA Location: Off Cenderawasih Bay, Papua, Indonesia A whale shark investigates the catch of a mobile net-fishing platform, known as a bagan. Lindbloom searched for sharks around dawn, using the bagan's bright lights to illuminate them when there was too little natural light for his drone. Category: Plants and Fungi Photographer: Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Papatsanis used ultrviolet light to illuminate mushrooms known as "beautiful bonnets" growing from a decaying log on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus in Greece. Category: Rising Star Award Photographer: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany Location: Germany and Northern Ireland, UK Tinker-Tsavalas uses macro photography to reveal the intricate details of tiny animals that are easily overlooked, particularly in urban habitats. His interest in macro photography developed during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when he was restricted to habitats close to his home in Berlin. Category: Natural Artistry Photographer: Michał Michalski, Poland Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Michalski used a slow shutter speed to photograph birds flying across a background of leafless birch trees. A field of unharvested sunflowers had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings, before they were startled into the air by a sparrowhawk. Category: Wetlands: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Visbal, Colombia Location: Stansbury Bay, Great Salt Lake, Utah, USA Visbal documents how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland as part of a long-term project on the industrial impact on waterways. The pink comes from microbes thriving in extremely salty water after the area was cut off from fresh water. Category: Photojournalism Photographer: Francisco Negroni, Chile Location: Route 40, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina Negroni records this scene of a dead puma displayed as a hunting trophy in Santa Cruz, a province in Argentine Patagonia. Although Santa Cruz banned puma hunting in 2025, illegal persecution continues. Category: Portfolio Award Photographer: Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK Location: West Sussex, England, UK Uddin's photographs explore the miniature world of slime moulds, organisms that can be barely visible to the naked eye and whose fruiting structures are just one to two millimetres high. A four-year study of children's photographs over the generations and archive material go on display. This is the second year of the UKAHT's three-year mission to protect the historic base on Goudier Island in Antarctica. The winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year captures a rarely seen elephant behaviour, revealing the complexity of their emotional lives. The Charity Commission says it is aware of "financial concerns" relating to the rare-breeds charity. Hoo Zoo and Dinosaur World has been keeping news of the latest arrival secret until now. title: 'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us': Student protesters speak to BBC in Paris
content: Students protests in France have entered their fourth week and with a renewed impetus, according to the BBC's James Waterhouse. The nationwide demonstrations against poor classroom conditions, including old buildings, teacher shortages and overcrowded classrooms, have caused disruption to education across France as hundreds of lycées (15-18 year-olds colleges) had to be closed. Students on the streets of Paris told the BBC that they had not achieved anything yet and that stopping now would be a "defeat". More on this story. The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians face another winter with electricity outages. Working with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, BBC Panorama reveals how the Russian billionaire hid his wealth with the help of Deloitte. Dramatic footage shows huge tornado moving through Marsala and Petrosino, causing damage to buildings and cars. A Kyiv resident told the BBC she has moved away from "everything that can be a Russian target" as Ukraine braces for another cold winter under intense attacks. The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases. A series of measures to tackle the housing crisis were defeated in parliament on Friday Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says the situation in Catalonia remains "very complicated". BBC Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson is near Kyiv's Northern Bridge, which has been hit for the second day in a row. The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is in Madrid, where a series of marches have been scheduled, after Spain's Congress rejected measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis. Turner’s early 19th century painting - Rome, from Mount Aventine - will be on display in the Italian capital for the first time ahead of an auction in London in December. The BBC's Paul Adams reports from the scene of the strike on Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences. All 29 people aboard the ship were safely evacuated using lifeboats, the Hellenic Coastguard said. The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay her rent set after it was increased by an investment firm. Russia's new drones are harder to intercept, making recent attacks on Ukraine even more devastating. Preliminary results suggest that Kremlin-backed United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority. Russia's parliamentary elections are under way, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. No casualties were reported after a Russian drone struck a train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials left the area. Thousands turned out to witness Céline Dion perform in Paris on Saturday, her first show after a six year illness-induced hiatus. Crowds have been flocking to the British Museum to see the Bayeux Tapestry as it's on public display in the UK for the first time since it was created nearly 1,000 years ago. Tens of thousands of people lined the streets to pay their respects after 13 days of national mourning. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
content: MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said. Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases. At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders". He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones. He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons. However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years. Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly". Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks. "With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said. "So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding." He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand." His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum , Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved". He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute". He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference. "I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters. Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK. The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities. Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites". Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique". He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK." The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police. Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard". The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response." Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia. On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual. "We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist." Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes". "These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on." Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are". He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities". In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely. Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism. He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent." Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK". He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil." The Hokkaido Shimbun journalist is accused of collecting information on Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo. Four years after the attacks, Serhii K will appear in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. It comes after Andy Burnham said Moscow had tried to interfere in the 2016 referendum. Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says. As election day looms, the president turns his eyes overseas for help with a pressing domestic problem. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Watch: Witnesses describe 'traumatic' moment man fell out of Six Flags rollercoaster
content: One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia. Six Flags Over Georgia park officials said staff found the man, identified as 42-year-old Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, beneath the ride. He was unresponsive and not breathing. Witnesses have spoken about the incident and its aftermath, with one man who was on the ride describing it as "super bizarre, traumatic". WATCH: The BBC's Nadine Yousif meets the separatists who want to quit the country - and the Canadians calling for unity in the face of threats from US President Trump. The US death row inmate's legal team said at a press conference that she is now "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution. The BBC's Sarah Smith details the injuries sustained by the US death row inmate after two failed lethal injections, and what comes next. Canada's Parti Québécois has promised it will hold the province's third vote on independence, but said they won’t do so until Donald Trump is out of office. The White House said Trump was warning of the risk a nuclear Iran with his comments at a Nebraska rally. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. The bodycam footage also shows a police officer finding a gun in Mangione's backpack, days after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. Governor Kathy Hochul said she is "deeply disturbed" by how the university's police handled the investigation and criticised the local prosecutor. title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
content: The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging". William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene. In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication". His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process." City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed. "William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said. The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time". "The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued. "The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did." A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers. The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation and ongoing closure of the park. An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in. Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass. Chapman was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe. "We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the school said in a tribute on Tuesday. "It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him." "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time," the statement continued. As a child, Chapman appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd. He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories. Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park have separately said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" are with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to Chapman's family and those who were at the scene. title: Man killed in tiger attack identified as William Chapman
content: The man who was killed by a tiger after entering its enclosure at a wildlife park has been identified as William Chapman, the BBC understands. Chapman, who visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on his own, entered the enclosure shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to South Yorkshire Police. An eyewitness described seeing him wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in. Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass. A force spokesperson said his family was aware and was being supported by specialist officers. The park was evacuated after the incident and remains closed as investigations continue. Chapman, who was in his mid-20s, was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe. As a child, he appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd. He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories. In a social media statement, a spokesperson for the stage school said: "We are deeply saddened to hear of the passing of our former student William Chapman. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time. "We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us. "It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him." They added that Chapman would be "truly missed" and he would "always hold a special place in our hearts". City of Doncaster Council earlier confirmed it had launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death, which a spokesperson said was "in line with our statutory duties". Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" were with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised. Chapman was reported to have entered the enclosure after climbing down from a walkway. Those who saw the attack said some witnesses had tried unsuccessfully to distract the tiger . A video posted on a social media account believed to be Chapman's appears to show the moments before the attack. In the footage, shot on a mobile phone, the inside of the enclosure can be seen as he approaches the tiger - perched on a wooden platform - across a patch of grass. The account has since been removed. A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an "urgent review" into "how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next". Dr Campbell Murn, a previous member of the government's zoo expert committee and lecturer at the University of Reading, said while it was a tragic incident, determined people could get inside zoo enclosures. "I view it in the same way a determined thief will get into somebody's house or somebody's car and despite the best security systems and enclosures sometimes these things happen," he said. Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack. She described seeing Chapman by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in". A few minutes later, she saw he had "climbed up onto the barriers". A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there". Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of him, and he was "shouting for help". She estimated about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area and, shortly afterwards, the park. She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?" "I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said. Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated. She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above. Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure." She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised".
