title: Actress Selma Blair faces charges for kicking nurse and officer after plane incident
content: US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight. Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board. While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star's attorney asked the judge to consider the actress's "body of work", and called Blair the "gold standard." The judge said she should not "get special treatment". Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail. She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct". As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said. Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US. The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane. One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse. At her arraignment in Queens, Blair's attorney Shawn Barnes asked the judge for leniency. He said that "violence" is "not who she is" and asked for the judge to consider her body of work. The actress is somebody that people she look up to, he said, referring to her as "the gold standard". The judge denied his request and said she "should not get special treatment...because she is a celebrity". The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond with the next hearing scheduled for 19 January. It is unclear when a date will be set for the federal case against her, which concerns the allegations of assault aboard the aircraft. title: White House ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece
content: Kimberly Guilfoyle, the embattled US ambassador to Greece, has been forced out of her job by the White House following a string of reports about alleged misconduct, marking a sudden and spectacular downfall for a high-profile figure in the MAGA movement with close ties to President Donald Trump’s family. New press secretary Katie Zacharia said in her first press briefing Tuesday that the White House had “asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” adding, “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her luck.” Later on Tuesday, the White House received Guilfoyle’s formal resignation, a White House official told CNN. “I didn’t like what I read,” Trump said, explaining why Guilfoyle had been removed. He added that he had not spoken with Guilfoyle personally. In a lengthy post on X , Guilfoyle acknowledged her time “may be coming to an end,” while disputing the recent allegations against her. “I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she wrote. Guilfoyle’s ouster comes following reports that she sought money in exchange for providing access to administration figures before she was confirmed to her position, accepted lavish gifts as ambassador and brought a lobbyist for a Greek construction company into official meetings. Lawyers for Guilfoyle have denied the allegations about seeking money and said reports about her travel were misleading, adding that she complied with federal gift and reporting requirements. While administration officials had signaled public discomfort with Guilfoyle’s alleged misconduct since the reports first emerged, she appeared reluctant to resign throughout the weekend and had been working to rally support among some administration officials, people familiar with the matter said. Even before the allegations first became public, she began reaching out to allies in and around the administration, asking for help navigating the impending story, sources familiar with the matter told CNN. Guilfoyle initially told some allies in the administration that the reporting was inaccurate, and her lawyers later claimed she was seeking to recoup debts when she asked a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill. Guilfoyle insisted that the donor was lying and that it was all a misunderstanding — claiming that the donor owed her money and it was not “pay-for-play.” Going into the weekend, she told allies that she would not resign, and claimed that she had been told she would not be fired, two sources told CNN. But her efforts did little to tamp down on frustrations about the reports, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in particular was eager to see her gone, the people familiar said. “She was basically fired on live TV,” one source said. Eric Deters, a former Trump donor, said Guilfoyle asked him in a text message to wire her $100,000 to pay off an American Express card in the days before her Senate confirmation. She said she would be his “ride or die” in the Trump administration if he did it, Deters said. “No question it was a quid pro quo,” Deters told CNN’s Jake Tapper last week. Deters did not wire Guilfoyle the money, saying he didn’t have the liquid assets at the time. Lawyers for Guilfoyle said in a statement to CNN that Deters owed Guilfoyle money for speeches and consulting work and called his statements false. “When Ms. Guilfoyle was preparing to leave private life for public service, she did what any professional does and tried to close out her outstanding receivables. Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption,” her lawyers wrote. In her post on X, Guilfoyle similarly said the allegations against her were “false.” “I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she wrote. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.” Guilfoyle was engaged for four years to the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. — though the president said Tuesday she “wasn’t a member of my family” and only “dated my son a long time ago.” After she and Donald Trump Jr.’s split, she was tapped to serve as ambassador to Greece and took on the role in September 2025. The president said Monday he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle. “We’re looking at it — yeah. We’re not happy,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House. Rubio was traveling to Greece when the reports of her alleged “pay-for-play” scheme were first reported by the Wall Street Journal . Guilfoyle attended multiple events with Rubio, and at the time he refused to comment on the reports. The Journal earlier reported on her alleged promotion of a Greek energy firm for regional energy deals. During the trip to Athens, Rubio praised Guilfoyle as a “strong ambassador here” and rebuffed questions about the reports of her misconduct. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said before he boarded his plane to leave the country, with Guilfoyle looking on. But privately, one source familiar with the matter said, Rubio expressed annoyance that Guilfoyle seemed intent on appearing at every event alongside him. The reports triggered questions and calls for investigations from Democrats on Capitol Hill. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for Guilfoyle to come before the committee and said that “ it must be determined whether Ambassador Guilfoyle solicited funds from any other source.” Following Tuesday’s announcement that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, the House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats noted that “resigning does not shield her from accountability. “Guilfoyle used her position as a Trump official to get rich, while American families struggle with the cost of living,” the committee wrote on X . “Congress must conduct oversight to understand how this happened and hold the admin accountable.” The State Department’s Office of the Inspector General is investigating Guilfoyle amid the misconduct allegations, according to source familiar with the effort. “As a matter of policy, OIG does not confirm, deny, or comment on investigative matters,” an inspector general spokesperson said. It is unclear what will happen with the investigation following her ouster. According to a source familiar with the workings of inspector general offices, it may depend on whether the Department of Justice opens an investigation into her alleged misconduct. If not, the State Department inspector general may continue its work, but its findings could take a year or so to complete. CNN’s Kit Maher contributed to this report. This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Trump’s foreign policy, Epstein and corruption allegations loom over Senate debates in Maine, Georgia and Iowa
content: One Republican tried to put distance between herself and President Donald Trump on trade and the Iran war. Another focused her criticism on Trump’s diesel deal with Russia. And a third tried to turn one of the GOP’s biggest political liabilities against their Democratic rival. Tuesday’s Senate debates in Maine, Georgia and Iowa offered a revealing look at how Republicans are navigating a difficult political environment in the closing weeks before the midterm elections, with control of the narrowly divided Senate at stake. In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins emphasized her independence from Trump as she sparred with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson over the Iran war, healthcare cuts and a trade war with Canada. Down the East Coast in Georgia, Republican Rep. Mike Collins went on the offensive as he tried to turn the tables by attacking Sen. Jon Ossoff over his ties to a donor named in the Jeffrey Epstein files — an issue that has largely put Republicans on the defensive. In another closely watched contest in Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek made their case to voters Tuesday night for the state’s open Senate contest, squabbling over Trump’s foreign policy and which of the two candidates actually showed up for work. The heated exchanges underscore the different challenges facing Republicans as they try to hold onto their Senate majority. Democrats, meanwhile, need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate. Here’s a look at key moments from the debates. In Maine, Susan Collins sought to emphasize her independence, as the five-term incumbent seeks reelection in an environment increasingly difficult for Republicans amidst the president’s plummeting popularity. After kicking off with her criticism of his approach to the war in Iran, Collins during later exchanges pointed to her vote against Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and her opposition to the tariffs on Canada. Her debate performance was the latest example of how vulnerable Republicans are defying Trump ahead of the midterms. When discussing the Iran war, Collins quickly called Trump out for not having a plan, and stressed how once the conflict surpassed 60 days, she voted against the war effort. “I voted with the Democrats to bring the war to an end, but there were not sufficient votes for that to happen,” the senator said. “In addition, I agree that the president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which part of the world’s oil travels, and I don’t feel that that was well anticipated, although it should have been.” While Jackson sought to tie Collins to her party’s signature tax and policy bill that cut Medicaid, Collins pointed out that she ultimately did not support the bill specifically because of those cuts. When Collins was asked about her position on Trump’s tariffs on Canada , she said, “I have been extremely outspoken in my opposition to Canadian tariffs and I have voted repeatedly to repeal them.” But while Collins sought to highlight her distance from Trump, she also argued that she was better equipped than Jackson to work with his administration, pointing to her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee as leverage in negotiations. Hinson similarly sought to distance herself from Trump during her Iowa debate on two of the biggest foreign policy crises confronting the president — Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war with Iran. On Tuesday night she criticized Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply markets with diesel fuel in a bid to lower prices that both candidates said are hurting Iowa farmers. “We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” she said. Hinson also pointed to a 2022 congressional ban on energy imports from Russia, a measure intended to punish the Russian economy over Putin’s decision to invade Ukraine. “I am proud to have voted for sanctions against Russia,” she said. “I’m banned from Russia because of my stance on being tough on them and supporting Ukraine, and we cannot allow Vladimir Putin to win that war.” She also said Trump’s war with Iran “does need to come to a resolute and successful end as quickly as possible.” However, Hinson balked when asked whether she would again vote against a war powers resolution that would halt Trump’s ability to continue military action against Iran without the approval of Congress. “I don’t think we need another resolution on the House floor. I think the president and the US military can bring it to the end,” she said. Those breaks with Trump were notable in a debate in which Trump played a minor role — a reality owing to both Hinson’s awareness of Trump’s sagging popularity and Turek’s need to win over a share of voters who backed Trump in the 2024 election. Hinson rarely made direct reference to Trump. But she did say she lobbied Trump personally last week to quickly get soybean trade pacts negotiated to open up foreign markets for Midwestern farmers — an acknowledgement of the economic fallout of Trump’s tariff policies. Mike Collins spent the first Georgia Senate debate largely on the defensive. But in Tuesday’s debate, he came out swinging. “This is a race between Georgia and Georgetown,” Collins said at the top of his opening state. From there, Collins called Ossoff a “globetrotting trust-fund kid,” and a “coward” who hides behind “scripted online clips.” And days after Ossoff opened their last debate by telling Georgians he would put Collins’ record on trial, the Republican said it was his turn to expose his opponent’s past. “Tough questions are going to come out tonight,” Collins said. “No one’s ever challenged Jon Ossoff on anything he’s ever voted on.” Collins, who faces an uphill climb to knock off the incumbent Democrat, spent much of the next hour criticizing Ossoff over his record on immigration, his support for green energy initiatives and the help he’s received from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman. He accused Ossoff of being an inadequate ally of Israel and of ignoring the interests of Georgians while he built a national profile that has fueled speculation about a future White House bid. “He’s using us as a platform,” Collins said in his closing remarks. “Georgians are hardworking people, and we deserve a senator that will work as hard as us for us.” For his part, Ossoff picked up where he left off at last week’s debate. He confronted Collins over his White nationalist son-in-law , criticized his support for Trump’s tariffs and tied him to the unpopular conflict with Iran. He also repeatedly pressed Collins to testify in a House ethics investigation into whether his office misused taxpayer funds. Collins called the investigation a “political hit job” when asked. Ossoff contended he was dodging. A testy back-and-forth in the Georgia Senate debate over files related to Jeffrey Epstein illustrated how the late financier’s crimes continue to roil American politics. During the debate, Mike Collins attacked Ossoff over the donations he’s received from Hoffman — “the same guy that’s in the Epstein files.” (After the Justice Department’s Epstein files showed several messages between Hoffman and Epstein, the prolific Democratic donor acknowledged he had multiple meetings with the disgraced financier. “I only knew Jeffrey Epstein because of a fundraising relationship with MIT, which I very much regret,” Hoffman wrote on X .) “The Epstein class is on stage right now, and it’s you,” Collins said, pressing Ossoff to denounce Hoffman. Ossoff shot back that Collins was against making the Epstein files public, a reference to a July 2025 House vote that blocked a measure that would have required the Department of Justice to release the records in 30 days. Collins ultimately joined 426 of his colleagues to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act last November after Trump, who had initially opposed the legislation, reversed and said he would sign the measure. Millions of documents were eventually released. “You voted to cover up the evidence, even though you knew 14-year-old girls had been raped, because Donald Trump told you to,” Ossoff said. “Donald Trump, who, by the way, is named 1,000 times in the Epstein files.” The debate around the documents and their ultimate revelations of Epstein’s ties to many high-profile figures dominated headlines for months over the last year. Now, candidates are seeking to capitalize on the issue, from the debate stage in Georgia to campaign ads in Colorado featuring the family of a prominent Epstein accuser. Both candidates tried to land an anti-corruption argument as the issue has taken center stage in the Maine Senate race When Collins attacked Jackson for being ineffective in cutting fraud in Medicare and Medicaid in the Maine state legislature, Jackson immediately turned the issue back on Collins. Jackson used Collins’ decision to talk about fraud as an opening to bring up a ProPublica report of a pay-to-play scheme allegation that Collins committed to steering millions of dollars in federal contracts to a Hawaii-based defense contractor in exchange for donations to her 2020 campaign. “I’m shocked that you’re talking about fraud because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI,” Jackson said. Collins has denounced the report as a “political hit job” and her office has called the allegations “categorically false.” Central to Jackson’s argument throughout the debate were accusations that the longtime incumbent is beholden to billionaires and special interests. Collins said that Jackson was insulting her integrity and tried to flip the script by later accusing Jackson of not being forthcoming about who is funding his campaign since he replaced Graham Platner on the ballot this summer. “I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning,” Jackson said, ahead of the FEC third quarter filing deadline on Thursday. In both of their Iowa Senate debates, Hinson and Turek have hammered each other for what they didn’t do. Early in their clash Tuesday night, Hinson repeatedly lambasted Turek for missing 58% of the Iowa House’s floor votes in the most recent legislative session. “That’s two out of every five days of work,” Hinson said. “If you show up to work two out of five days, you don’t get a promotion; you’re getting fired.” Turek’s defense for those missed votes was that he was campaigning for the Senate. Before facing Hinson in the general election, he had to win a competitive primary. “I’m out campaigning. I’m out meeting Iowans all over — all 99 counties. I’ve done hundreds of in-person town halls,” he said. Turek, meanwhile, criticized Hinson for failing to conduct in-person public town halls — a decision many congressional Republicans have made after seeing the fierce backlash to Trump’s second term at early 2025 town halls. He said Hinson is “the least bipartisan member of the Iowa delegation.”

title: James Talarico has Democrats dreaming big after decades of dashed hopes in Texas
content: Democrats have been dreaming big in Texas for decades, awash in optimism that this could finally be the year to win a US Senate seat. For the first time, lifelong Republican Pete Nodecker is joining them, planning to cast his ballot for James Talarico when early voting begins here next week. “I’m rather disillusioned with the Republican Party,” said Nodecker, 81, a retired restaurant supplier. “The Republican Party has been hijacked. They’re not the Republican Party that I was a member of for all my life.” In the final three weeks of the fall campaign, Talarico is seeking to build a coalition of voters to break a 38-year streak of Democrats falling short in their bid for Senate. He’s hoping to tap into the dissatisfaction of voters like Nodecker, who twice voted for Donald Trump, while motivating Democrats to believe in his ability to defeat GOP nominee Ken Paxton. “I’m a Democrat in Texas, so we’re always a little bit nervous,” said Sue Reed, a member of the Tarrant County Democratic Woman’s Club. “But I would say this has been the most positive vibe and energy that we’ve seen in years.” The modern ritual of Democratic optimism in Texas dates to at least 2002, when the party put together a “Dream Team” ticket led by former Dallas Mayor Ron Kirk, who ran for Senate. In 2014, Democratic state Sen. Wendy Davis drew national fanfare as she ran for governor after a high-profile filibuster against abortion restrictions. Four years later, Beto O’Rourke shattered fundraising records and drew massive crowds as he challenged Republican Sen. Ted Cruz. Through it all, Democrats came up short — and sometimes very short. O’Rourke remains the high-water mark, losing to Cruz by less than 3 percentage points. This year’s Senate contest has become one of the marquee races in the fight for control of the chamber, a leading example of how Republicans are scrambling to defend deeply red terrain. The seat almost certainly would not have been competitive if Paxton hadn’t defeated Sen. John Cornyn in the May primary runoff. Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative, was born the year after the last Democratic senator from Texas, Lloyd Bentsen, was reelected in 1988. He has inspired sanguine Democrats and won over some Republicans frustrated by the president and their party. “He impresses me because he’s willing to take questions from all sides,” said Glen Whitley, a retired Tarrant County judge, who has urged his fellow Republicans to “put country over party” and support Talarico. “I’m ashamed that Ken Paxton is even on the ballot.” Paxton and his allies in Washington have launched a furious, nine-figure advertising campaign to paint Talarico as too liberal for Texas. They have especially seized on his past comments about gender and religion, such as his remark during a 2021 legislative debate that “God is nonbinary.” He has since admitted that some of his comments “missed the mark” and has sought to moderate his views on transgender issues. Paxton has accused Talarico of undergoing a political makeover to hide his true views from Texans. “California already has two senators. They don’t need a third,” Paxton says in a staple of his stump speech. Republicans are scrambling to unify their ranks against Talarico. Paxton said in a speech Friday that there are “a lot of apathetic Republicans” right now, suggesting it was due to the Iran war, and Trump has said he is “worried” about the race. In one conversation after another, Democratic voters in Texas were upbeat at Talarico’s prospects over Paxton, even as some acknowledged an air of caution that the state’s long pattern of voting GOP could dash Democratic hopes. “I think what’s different is that James has done such a great job of tapping into what a lot of people are upset about,” said Laura Leeman, a Democratic voter in Fort Worth. “And not just from one party or the other.” As she attended a Democratic fundraising event at a Fort Worth gallery, Joyce Franklin said she was working to stay positive in the final weeks of a nail-biting campaign. “I’m trying to remain as optimistic as I can without being totally let down,” Franklin said, recalling the devastation she felt in 2024 when Trump won a second term. “I don’t want to set myself up for that disappointment again, but I think this time we finally have the right formula to move forward.” The grandson of a pastor and a seminary student himself, Talarico talks far more about faith than most Democrats. As he campaigns, he sprinkles in verses from the Gospel of Luke, along with the argument that love is a stronger motivating force than hate. “His faith is important to him, and that’s something we don’t always see in Democratic candidates,” said Jill Fox, a Democratic voter from River Oaks. “I think that’s an interesting dynamic that’s attracting some independents and maybe even some crossover Republicans.” Talarico has a master’s degree in theological studies from the Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary and is training to become an ordained minister. A former middle school teacher in San Antonio, Talarico entered politics in 2018 when he ran for a Republican-held seat in the northern suburbs of Austin. The 29-year-old’s win made him the youngest member of the Texas Legislature at the time. He quickly established himself as an advocate for public education and other bread-and-butter issues. However, he found himself competing for more liberal voters after Republican redistricting forced him to seek reelection in 2022 in an Austin-based district. It was around that period that Talarico began voicing more progressive views on social issues — and offering some of the comments that he now refers to as “cringey.” Republicans are working hard to make sure their voters do not forget those moments. Marvin Rodak, who owns a coffee roasting and auto repair business in Fort Worth, said he was carefully following the Senate race and remained undecided as the campaign entered the home stretch. He said he was frustrated by the tariff whiplash from the Trump administration and record diesel prices, but also uncertain that he wanted to see Democrats control the Senate. “The true Democratic Party is fading,” said Rodak, 75, who was raised in a Democratic household and became a Republican as an adult. “Democrats need to distance themselves from socialism.” He said he was concerned by Paxton’s legal and political baggage , but not sold on Talarico’s ability to do the job without undue influence from Democratic leaders. He said he intended to carefully study both candidates before reaching a decision. “I think every election is an opportunity to send a message,” Rodak said. Rodak is the kind of voter who Republicans are intensely targeting in the final weeks of the race, hopeful they will come home once they learn more about Talarico. From the start of September through Election Day, Republican-aligned groups are planning to spend $232 million — more than they’re set to spend on competitive Senate campaigns in Michigan and Maine combined. The bulk of the outside spending by the GOP has come from Texas PAC, a group affiliated with the Senate Leadership Fund, the top Republican super PAC in Senate races. “If you care about your children, do not vote for James Talarico,” a woman says in one ad, suggesting Talarico supports gender-affirming surgery for minors. Talarico voted against a 2023 bill prohibiting gender-affirming care for minors, but he now says he opposes surgeries and opposed the bill because it was too broad. In an ad of his own, he faces the camera directly and says: “No, I don’t support sex-change surgeries for kids.” In trying to shore up its voters, the GOP has even deployed Paxton’s estranged wife, Angela Paxton, to make the case that Republicans should stick with the entire ticket, even if they have reservations about specific candidates. In the final weeks of the race, Trump has focused relentlessly on Texas . On each of his last three visits, he has aggressively assailed Talarico, as he tries to rescue Paxton’s candidacy. Vice President JD Vance appeared with Paxton on Tuesday in East Texas, a deep-red region where the candidate needs his base to turn out in large numbers. “We cannot elect Tala-freako to the US Senate,” Vance said, repeating an insult Trump has repeatedly used against Talarico. Nodecker, who voted for Trump in 2016 and 2020 but became infuriated by him after his response to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, said he believes Trump’s frequent trips to Texas could backfire and motivate his critics more than his remaining loyalists. “If anything,” Nodecker said, “it persuades me to go the opposite direction even more.”

title: Judge says Trump press ban likely violates First Amendment
content: The Trump administration must allow CNN, MS NOW, and Politico to access the White House while their lawsuit over the president’s press ban plays out, a federal judge ruled on Tuesday. US District Judge Tim Kelly said that President Donald Trump’s press ban likely violated the First Amendment, expanding upon his previous legal rationale for ordering that the three outlets be allowed access to the White House. He wrote that Trump’s own comments explaining the ban show a “likely causal link between Plaintiffs’ protected First Amendment speech and his revocation of their hard passes.” Those comments helped the outlets prove that Trump had banned them for retaliatory reasons, in violation of the First Amendment, Kelly said. “President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” the judge wrote. Kelly’s latest order sets the stage for the Trump administration to appeal the case. His previous order that blocked the White House ban was set to expire Tuesday. The judge’s new order rejected the Justice Department’s claims that national security concerns at least partially motivated Trump’s ban. He wrote that there was “no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision.” Kelly, who was appointed to the bench by Trump in his first term, said that Trump’s comments led him to believe that the ban amounted to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. Kelly, in an earlier phase of the case, had ordered the administration to reactivate the press badges used by the news organizations for due process reasons — meaning that the outlets were not given fair notice of the ground rules before their access was revoked. His opinion Tuesday referenced letters the White House sent the outlets after their lawsuit was already filed, which ostensibly explained why Trump was banning them, while giving the outlets a deadline to respond. Kelly concluded those letters did not do enough to fix those issues — in part because they were sent after the ban was put into effect. CNN has reached out to the White House and Justice Department for comment. Ted Boutrous, the attorney for the media outlets, celebrated the ruling in a statement Tuesday, saying, “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.” “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” Boutrous added. Before getting into the meat of his opinion, Kelly said that his ruling shouldn’t be construed as leaving the government “powerless” to respond to reporting that unlawfully discloses classified information, as he expressed some sympathy for Trump’s concerns. “[N]o one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed,” he wrote. The judge went on to write that he took “seriously” the government’s interest in protecting classified information. But he could find “just about no evidence in the record to explain or justify the ‘ban’ from a national security perspective.” He noted that the administration did not try to submit any information — even under seal or just for the court to view — that would have bolstered the Justice Department’s national security arguments. “In the end, Defendants do not even bother to identify what specific information in any of these ‘reporting incidents’ was allegedly classified or sensitive,” Kelly wrote. Trump has repeatedly defended the ban since he announced it on September 18. He has pointed to his perceptions that the outlets’ coverage was “negative” or “one-sided” in explaining why he wanted to block the journalists from accessing the White House. However, in court filings, the Justice Department has claimed that there was also a national security rationale for the ban, citing stories by the outlets covering the Iran war, the East Wing ballroom construction and even the midterm GOP convention. The news organizations have argued that the ban not only affected their ability to cover the president, but also had a chilling effect on other outlets. At a hearing in the case last Thursday, Kelly signaled skepticism of the dueling rationales Trump and Justice Department lawyers had provided for why the president wanted to ban the media outlets from the White House. Kelly remarked at the hearing that it was “unusual” to have a case where “the decision maker seems to have said … I am taking this action because ‘x’ and ‘y,’” and now the government is saying, “it’s ‘z.’” Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik told the judge that it’s “within the discretion of the president” to remove reporters or news outlets from the White House. Velchik said “CNN has been on notice for years” and that Trump has long been calling the outlet “fake news.” “Trump doesn’t mind negative press stories if he deserves them,” Velchik added. Boutrous emphasized the subjective nature of the ban and how Trump made the decision himself. “We know what he decided. He said it over and over again,” Boutrous said. “He issued the ban himself.” Boutrous added, “the only thing I can come up with” is that the president likely “woke up on the wrong side of the bed” and decided to issue the ban. This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Trump debates calling off livestream of firing squad execution after learning Fort Hood shooter was paralyzed
content: President Donald Trump and his advisers are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter, with Trump having remarked privately that he did not initially know that Nidal Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down, two sources familiar with the discussions told CNN. The president was not aware that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was announcing last week that the administration planned to let the public watch the execution, the sources said, and was not sure what to make of it at first. Trump was, however, firmly behind the decision to execute Hasan via firing squad , multiple officials told CNN, and he’s often defended it in public. And even after Hegseth posted on X on Thursday confirming that the Pentagon planned to livestream the execution, Trump polled several of his advisers and allies about how to proceed. It was during the those conversations that Trump learned Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down — he was shot in the back by law enforcement during the 2009 shooting at Ford Hood — and that he now uses a wheelchair, the sources said, which made showing the execution publicly less palatable to the president. One of the sources familiar with the discussions pointed to Trump’s deep understanding of imagery as a key reason why he may decide to ditch plans for the livestream. The president has also listened to the argument that a public execution by firing squad could serve as propaganda for foreign adversaries and terrorists to try to paint Hasan as a martyr, a Trump adviser told CNN. The White House on Tuesday referred CNN to the president’s comments on Saturday in which he acknowledged “two thoughts” about what to do and said he’d make the ultimate decision. “He was vicious. He was violent,” Trump told reporters about Hasan over the weekend. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So, I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.” The Pentagon is also reevaluating plans to fully livestream the execution, according to a source familiar with the discussions. Even if there is a broadcast of the event, the source said, it will likely be cut before shots are fired, in part, due to concerns that the moment could offer a propaganda opportunity for terrorist groups. Hegseth’s office has not responded to additional requests for comment about whether plans to livestream the execution have changed. The plan to livestream the execution has faced bipartisan backlash, and people across the Pentagon and the Army were caught off guard, CNN has previously reported . Trump told reporters on Friday that he was not involved but said, “I understand the decision,” adding that some people “want to set an example” by livestreaming the execution. Hegseth had initially recommended death by firing squad for Hasan — who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding dozens of others — and Trump approved it. The execution, which is scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the US Army’s first such execution of a soldier since World War II and its first imposition of any death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years. A US-born citizen of Palestinian descent, Hasan said he was targeting soldiers he was set to deploy with to Afghanistan and wanted to protect the Taliban and its leaders from the US military.

title: Trump admin silent as Russia hits American businesses with ‘drones and missiles’ in Ukraine
content: As President Donald Trump and his administration have ratcheted up pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, citing harm to American consumers, they have remained silent on recent Russian strikes on US businesses in Ukraine. Russia has escalated its attacks on facilities tied to American corporations – and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine writ large – over the past several months. According to Andy Hunder, the President of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine, Russian missiles and drones have damaged facilities belonging to some of America’s most notable brands, including Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, McDonalds and Oreo. Although Russia has tried to deter successful American business in the past, it’s “nothing we’ve seen like over the last months,” Hunder told CNN. “This is a direct hit with drones and missiles, and they keep hitting them. It’s sending a message that they’re targeting American business. We’re not seeing any response from the White House,” he said. “We need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors that are being hit and are being targeted,” he said. When a Russia drone struck a Coca-Cola factory outside Kyiv in early September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attack was a “clear signal” to the US. “Today, the Russians struck a Coca-Cola plant with a drone. Coca-Cola has become such an enemy to them that they’re burning it down with their Shaheds,” Zelensky said in his nightly video address on September 3, referring to “Iranian-designed ​drones.” “This is a clear signal from Russia to America. The Russians cannot possibly be unaware that this is an American enterprise,” Zelensky added. Later that month, the Russians used “an attack drone” to destroy a warehouse used by McDonald’s, Zelensky said in a post on X . McDonald’s Ukraine confirmed in a statement that “a warehouse operated by one of our logistics partners in the Kyiv region was damaged in a drone attack on 25 September.” “An attack drone – against ordinary food products,” he wrote. “The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers – for Russia, ordinary life in and of itself is simply a target.” McDonald’s Ukraine said that as a result of the damage, its restaurants are offering a reduced menu. PepsiCo acknowledged in a statement in late August that a production facility in the Mykolaiv region was damaged, but there were no casualties. There is not a consensus among the US businesses on the ground about how much they want to talk publicly about being hit “or disclose the fact that they’ve been targeted multiple times,” a former senior State Department official told CNN. “Some businesses do want us to raise this,” Hunder echoed, but others “are treading very carefully.” However, several Democratic US lawmakers have publicly called on the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and to call out Moscow’s actions. Ukraine has highlighted the attacks as another reason to step up defense support, so that they can sufficiently shield American companies on the ground. The Chamber of Commerce meets with visiting US lawmakers from both parties when they visit Kyiv, and Hunder told CNN they have asked them to raise the matter with the White House. President Donald Trump spoke out publicly when asked in August 2025 about a Russian strike on a US electronics factory, saying he told Russian President Vladimir Putin that he was “not happy about it.” A White House official said Trump “wants the war to stop entirely so the senseless killing ends.” “The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done,” the official said, arguing that the US is “the only country in the world” that can “play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end.” Still, the relative lack of condemnation on the strikes from the Trump administration stands in contrast to the admonishments to the Ukrainian government about striking Russian energy infrastructure. In February, CNN reported the administration had warned Kyiv that its strikes on a Russian Black Sea oil facility late last year had impacted US investments in Kazakhstan. In recent weeks, Trump has blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian diesel facilities for rising fuel prices, which have been driven up by the US-Iran war. Last Friday, he announced a deal to waive sanctions and purchase diesel from Russia, in defiance of US law. The US has also threatened to restrict intel sharing and munitions for Ukraine if Kyiv does not stop those strikes, sources told CNN. Hunder told CNN he has struggled to understand the administration’s relative silence on the matter, particularly given how much they’ve portrayed themselves as pro-US business. “Any company, any business, wants to have some sort of protection. You would expect your government to stand up in your corner and fight the fight with you, especially if it’s a foreign military that is attacking the American companies,” he said. The former senior State Department official noted that “there’s an awful lot of people in ‘official Washington’ who think the only people who can talk about Ukraine are Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and if it’s not one of the two of them, then we need to stay out of it.” As such, it is a challenge to even draw attention to the attacks on US businesses. “The idea that you would get a rationale back” on why the US was silent about the attacks “is not something that people can expect,” they told CNN. Hunder said the American Chamber of Commerce sent a message seeking a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner last month to update them on the state of US business in Ukraine, including the latest hits on American business. “We didn’t get any response on that,” he said.

title: White House officials question how long Katie Zacharia can last after ‘brutal’ press briefing
content: Several White House officials are questioning how long Katie Zacharia will keep the press secretary job after her first briefing Tuesday, saying her performance was unlikely to satisfy President Donald Trump. Several advisers and officials offered negative reviews of the briefing to CNN, with one characterizing it as “brutal.” Others described it as unusual, awkward, stilted and, at times, uncomfortable. Zacharia appeared at the podium for only about 15 minutes, and most of that time was dedicated to an opening statement touting Trump’s accomplishments. She called on only three reporters for questions before ending the briefing. Some White House officials and Trump advisers expressed confusion about why the White House rushed Zacharia to the podium. A source familiar with the matter said Trump had asked Zacharia to conduct the briefing, and while some in his orbit had misgivings, the source was unaware of anyone relaying them to Zacharia or Trump. “She should have been doing murder boards for two weeks before going up there,” one Trump adviser told CNN, before critiquing Zacharia’s performance. “The best thing she did was break the news about [Ambassador to Greece Kimberly] Guilfoyle — at least that takes the focus off of her performance.” “Why did they put her out there so quickly?” a White House official said incredulously. “Literally zero reason to put her out on her second day, unprepared.” Trump praised Zacharia after the briefing, telling reporters shortly after: “I thought she was very good.” White House communications director Steven Cheung also said in a statement to CNN that “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team.” Zacharia planned ahead of time that she would give lengthy introductory remarks, based on what Trump had requested, and take only take three questions – from outlets she chose ahead of time, a source familiar with the matter said. The briefing was notably shorter than what had become the norm. Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt’s briefings lasted for about an average of 45 minutes. During her first briefing, she called on two “new media” reporters before an Associated Press correspondent. She would also take questions from reporters standing in the aisles. Zacharia called on reporters from conservative outlet Breitbart, which was in the “new media” seat, Fox News and the Daily Mail. She appeared to have their names written down ahead of time. Trump and Zacharia met briefly ahead of the briefing, and Trump told her he was seeking Guilfoyle’s resignation, a source said. Another adviser told CNN that while Zacharia “wasn’t great,” it was just her first press briefing. They expected Trump would give her the benefit of the doubt. Trump had grown somewhat infatuated with Zacharia’s appearances on Fox News before eventually hiring her, sources told CNN. But one of the advisers noted that appearing on a cable TV panel and standing in front of the world at the podium were two different things. “No question we’re all missing Karoline,” said one adviser. Zacharia said she was cutting the briefing short because Trump would likely soon take reporter questions on the White House South Lawn before he departed for Alaska. “I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there,” she said. Questions have also surfaced online about Zacharia’s status as an attorney , and CNN has found no evidence that she has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating Pepperdine Caruso School of Law. When Trump announced her new role, he referred to his new press secretary as “an attorney.” “The State Bar of California has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black having been licensed to practice law in California,” a spokesperson for the California State Bar told CNN in a statement, referring to her maiden name. “Due to confidentiality requirements, the State Bar can only confirm whether someone passed the bar exam, not whether they took the bar exam.” When a reporter pressed Trump at the White House on Tuesday morning about what state Zacharia passed the bar exam in, the president turned to his new press secretary, who was standing behind him. “Which state?” Trump asked Zacharia. She responded that she had moved to China. In response to questions on her legal credentials, a White House official told CNN that Zacharia moved to China with her husband after graduating law school, citing his job at an American private equity firm, and that she worked on international transaction law at the time. The official did not respond to a follow-up question about whether she passed the bar exam. According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia worked as an associate on the international practice team at Zhong Lun Law in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013. She was also general counsel to Fix California , an elections-focused nonprofit founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell, from January 2024 to March 2025. Her most recent position was senior communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group. It is unclear on what cadence Zacharia will brief reporters. A CNN Reliable Sources analysis of the White House video archive found Leavitt, who departed the role in August, held formal briefings about once a week on average before having her second child. She held 14 briefings in the four months leading up to her maternity leave in late April. She held another 49 briefings through the rest of 2025, which included several nontraditional briefings. This story and headline have been updated with additional reporting.

title: Archbishop serving US military urges Catholics be excused from proposed firing squad execution
content: The archbishop assigned to serve Catholics in the US military strongly condemned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream a firing squad execution and said Monday that Catholic personnel should not participate. “As I would in the case of a procured abortion, I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Archbishop Timothy P. Broglio wrote in a statement , marking the latest dispute between the Trump administration and the Catholic Church . His comments came after he met with Pope Leo on Monday. The pontiff himself strongly condemned the death penalty over the weekend, consistent with the church’s opposition to capital punishment but also coming after the relatively new pope has already clashed with US President Donald Trump over issues of war, immigration and press freedom. Last week, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced in a podcast interview that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan would be shown in public . A Pentagon official later said the execution “will be livestreamed.” The decision to livestream a public firing squad execution was swiftly met with bipartisan concern and opposition — including from Republican members of Congress — as well as widespread condemnation from world leaders. He also made clear he felt for the loved ones of those impacted by Hasan’s 2009 mass shooting that killed 13 people, adding that he presided at the funeral for one of the victims of the attack. “I renew my expression of heartfelt sympathy to the families and friends of those who died in the attack at Fort Hood,” Broglio wrote. “It was an attack that disregarded the dignity of the human person.” Broglio questioned the purpose of making such an event public, calling on “all men and women of good will” to “do what is possible to keep the exposure to the live-streaming of the proposed execution from the vision of the young and impressionable.” “Will the exposure of a live-stream to the young and impressionable during the 250th anniversary year of our independence be able to be repaired?” Broglio asked in his statement. “The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world. Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world?”

title: ‘Pharma Bro’ Martin Shkreli has caught the attention of federal and state authorities again
content: “Pharma Bro” Martin Shkreli has caught the attention of federal and state authorities again. Since his 2022 release from prison for securities fraud, Shkreli — who gained national notoriety for inflating the price of a life-saving drug — has been livestreaming on YouTube his stock trades, including several positions involving pharmaceutical companies. In June, he launched a trading competition with an account boasting a $10 million balance and earlier touted a successful short position he had taken on a biotech company. The Federal Trade Commission and attorneys general from seven states alleged that through trading and statements on social media platforms, Shkreli has “flagrantly and repeatedly” violated the court order that barred him from participating in the pharmaceutical industry. On Tuesday, they asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt, fine him the total profits he made from the trades, and potentially send him to prison if he doesn’t stop. “In addition to his public trading, Shkreli himself has indicated that he has more accounts and does most of his trading off social media,” authorities wrote. They cited Shkreli saying, “I have some other accounts that I’[d] show you, but, like, I know feds are watching, so f*ck that,’” according to the court filing. The FTC and seven states — New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia — sued Shkreli in 2020 for anticompetitive behavior for raising the price of Daraprim, a life-saving drug for a toxic parasitic disease, by 4,000% overnight to $750 per pill. The case went to trial, and in January 2022, Shkreli was found liable, ordered to pay $64.6 million and banned from any activity in the pharmaceutical industry. The civil trial followed his separate criminal case in which Shkreli was found guilty of securities fraud in 2018 and sentenced to seven years in prison. He was released in May 2022. Almost immediately, the FTC and states allege, Shkreli began violating the court’s ban by setting up a trading competition involving at least 11 pharmaceutical stocks. He also started shorting, or betting the price of biotech company Cassava Sciences would drop. During his livestreams, authorities say, Shkreli argued the company’s clinical study was doomed to fail. On November 21, 2024, on X, he said, “I don’t think it doesn’t work. It is impossible for it to work.” Four days later, Cassava publicly said the clinical study failed. Authorities say Shkreli “gloated” about the success of his short position. “They don’t want you to know. They want you to stay stupid. I try to give you some advice. Twenty years of experience. I made a lot of money in these binary events, man. Some people say that I’m the GOAT at it, but you didn’t want to hear nothing,” Shkreli said, according to the court filing. CNN reached out to Shkreli for comment. His last livestream was on Monday. Authorities allege Shkreli’s sister and her partner appear to have assisted him. They asked the judge to order them to preserve evidence. The FTC and states say what they uncovered may be the “tip of the iceberg.” “We do not currently have access to the vast majority of evidence that would establish the extent of his misconduct, including how he has profited from his violations and whether he continues to own any Pharmaceutical Company stocks,” they wrote.

title: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
content: Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump. The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.” To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones. In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August. Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader , and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”. Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine , and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin. UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. He met Keir Starmer at Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, publicly berated the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago. During that trip Zelenskyy was also hosted by King Charles , who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits. Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones. These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv. In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. “My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe . “It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

title: Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms
content: Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, the head of MI5 said on Tuesday, but he added that did not mean the Kremlin had any impact on the result. Ken McCallum endorsed comments by Andy Burnham , who raised the issue over the past two days, though he said continuing to debate it risked giving the Kremlin a needless propaganda victory. During an annual threat update, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency said the Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” with biased anti-migration and anti-EU reports. He said there had also been “a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”: an unspecified number of fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, that had sought to influence the result. Neither tactic was particularly sophisticated or successful, the spy chief said. There was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. Both interference attempts have been previously cited in studies released in the years after the Brexit vote. The digital campaign group 89up said RT and Sputnik had published 261 mostly misleading articles highlighting immigration and other anti-EU issues that achieved 134m potential page impressions . Other studies have reported on a “troll army” of state-linked Russian accounts tweeting about the referendum in the run-up to the vote, though estimates of numbers active have varied wildly from 54 to 150,000 . Burnham had first returned to the issue on Sunday, during a podcast interview, though at first it was unclear whether the prime minister had been given new intelligence on a topic that had largely been considered forgotten. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” said the prime minister, implying he had a discussion or briefing on the issue. A day later, however, he backed off when challenged by the Conservatives on whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate, and he did not supply any additional information in the Commons. On Tuesday Downing Street said it had been confirmed that Russia interfered in the 2019 general election and it was “inconceivable that they didn’t in 2016”. But the prime minister’s spokesperson added: “We don’t believe it was successful in the British referendum in 2016.” Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion McCallum said it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was the subject of controversy for several more days. “It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us,” he said. Continued attention gave the impression that Kremlin disinformation attempts were more successful than they actually were, the MI5 chief added. “I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front-page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey,” he said.

title: Wes Streeting’s unintelligible jargon shows how well he’s bedded in at the MoD
content: W hen Andy Burnham announced his first cabinet in July, few would have had Wes Streeting marked down as a likely defence secretary. Not even Wes. And no one is more bullish about Wes’s life chances than Wes. It just didn’t seem a natural fit. Defence secretaries tend to be more the unsmiling types who operate in the shadows. Politicians like John Healey, with the pallor of someone who has spent too long in underground bunkers with military chief of staffs. People who slide in and out of rooms without making a fuss. Wes has always been someone who likes to be noticed. Enjoys the theatre of Westminster. The first to arrive at a party and the last to leave. A natural gossip. “Psst – you’ll never guess what Zelenskyy just said to Trump.” But in the past few months, Wes has had something of a personality change. At the recent Labour party conference, he kept his appearances distinctly low key. No longer the life and soul of Liverpool, out till 2am before getting up to do the media round just four hours later. It can’t be long before we see him driving a tank somewhere near the Russian border. Wes is gonna be Wes. He also has the distinct advantage of not being Penny Mordaunt , the former Tory minister who has done more to terrify a nation than any living defence secretary. A few weeks ago, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians in which Michael Gove was cast as the prime minister and Penny as defence secretary. The set up was that Russia had torpedoed a ship off Scotland, with the politicians and the military placed in a mock-up Cobra meeting and left to come up with responses as the situation developed. This could have been the moment to restore faith in our democratic institutions. To admire the insight and clarity with which our leaders handle a crisis. To see how they repay the trust and power which we bestow on them. In which case, you should think again. What actually emerged is that politicians are no brighter than the rest of us. They just have egos which make them believe they are the right people in the right place at the right time. And that we are lucky to have them. To put it bluntly, The War Game was a total shitshow. Just one bad decision after another. For the first two episodes, The Govester was like a rabbit in the headlights. Completely clueless as the UK came under increasing levels of attack. The best he could offer was to repeat back the last thing that was said to him and bark “ASAP!” Penny, though, was a total menace to herself and the country from the word go. If this is really how defence secretaries behave, we should all be out digging bunkers in open land and stocking up on tinned food. Not that it would do much good. From the outset, Penny was hell-bent on escalating the conflict despite being told Britain’s military defences were totally threadbare and that the UK was only a middle-ranking global power. She couldn’t wait to use up the UK’s arsenal of weapons, and by the end two nuclear warheads were 20 minutes away from annihilating two major cities. Bye bye Britain. Still, at least she would go down as our last ever defence secretary. So Streeting’s first appearance before the defence select committee was, first and foremost, a moment to give thanks he wasn’t Penny and that we are all – more or less – still here. And Wes looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD. He now talks mainly in letters – SDR, DIP and NAD – and jargon that is designed to be unintelligible to most mortals. Mostly, he wanted to get through the entire session by saying as little as possible and to send any stray reporters who had wandered into the committee room by mistake to sleep. He’d have liked to be more open, he said. But if he was, he’d have to kill us. For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets. If not exactly his happiest place, then still a happy one. Wes began by telling the committee that the UK and its Nato allies were facing their gravest threat since the cold war. Given that, you could understand why he wan’t particularly keen on telling us just how unprepared we were for some kind of an attack as our enemies might be listening. When Streeting had taken on the defence job he had spent most of the first week telling the media that he would – like his predecessor – resign if he thought the money being allocated was inadequate. Three months on and he was rather dancing on the head of a pin. He couldn’t say how, when or even if the commitment to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 would be met. We just had to keep the faith that somehow it would all work out OK. John Healey said it would all end up OK, and if John Healey said so then we ought to believe him. After all, it wasn’t just a question of spending more money – it was also about spending the money he did have better. It also turned out that some of our defence capacity was largely illusory. Both because it took six years for most military contracts to be delivered, by which time there was a fair chance the hardware would be obsolete, and because much of the increased spending had been backloaded until after the next election. Politicians never tire of passing on costs to future governments. The MoD’s permanent secretary, Jeremy Pocklington, spent at least five minutes trying to persuade the committee that backloading wasn’t really backloading even if it looked like backloading. For that kind of mind-numbing bullshit, Jezza has been awarded the Companion of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath. Still, Wes did say at one point that he “wasn’t keen on fighting a war”, which I suppose is a start. Gives him the edge over Penny at the very least.
